newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian opposition seeks to heal internal rifts.
newsitem.headline: Colombian opposition seeks to heal internal rifts.

text.p: Colombia's opposition Conservatives will seek to heal internal rifts and map out a strategy to win back power in the 1998 presidential election during their national convention, which opens on Tuesday.
The party has been divided since it suffered three electoral defeats in 1986, 1990 and 1994 at the hands of the Liberals, the other force in Colombia's de facto two-party system.
But analysts are hopeful that a truce could emerge among the warring factions at the convention.
Political analysts say the Conservatives must rally around a banner of opposition to President Ernesto Samper, tainted by alleged links to drug kingpins.

In addition, they must seek to exploit divisions within the Liberal Party -- which have worsened during the current crisis, sparked by the corruption scandal -- ahead of the 1998 presidential elections.

Conservative Sen. Juan Camilo Restrepo said on Sunday: "We can match the aspirations of the Colombian people better than any other party. The pendulum of modern history is swinging back toward a conservative vision of society. We must make a bid for power."
He called for all factions to unite behind a consensus candidate in elections to renew the party leadership but did not specify his preference.

Former President Misael Pastrana, a major figure in the mainstream party, and Sen. Enrique Gomez Hurtado, heir to a faction that formally split with Pastrana in 1990, could emerge this week as possible contenders for the post.

But the current party chairman, Jaime Arias, dismissed such speculation on Sunday, saying: "I don't think we will see a consensus leader emerge, although it's an excellent idea. There's great rivalry between the regions and different sectors of the party. They already have their own candidates in mind."
Even if a new consensus leader does emerge, the rehabilitation of the Conservative Party will be no easy task.

The latest split came this year, when party rebels in Congress chose to back Samper and voted to clear him in June after a four-month inquiry into allegations that he funded his presidential campaign with millions of dollars from the Cali drug cartel.
While other Conservatives withdrew all support from the Samper administration, the rebels retained a series of minor posts. They are not expected to attend this week's convention.
